proof_attempt_summary: D0 derived the stable local QTE process, peak-location law, uniform block interval, and a clipping phase diagram; the final theorem graph is discharged and D0.5 math and decision reviewers passed without findings. The field-tier gate rejected the fully proved exact quadratic known-propensity benchmark at score 7.3 below the 7.4 cutoff. A field-tier continuation would require a new proposal architecture, such as broader assignment geometry or a minimax peak-estimation result; this run stopped before Lean formalization under the fixed field floor.
tldr: Weak overlap changes the local geometry of the estimated QTE peak. At the known quadratic propensity \(e(x)=x^2/2\), an \(n^{-1/4}\) percentile window produces a two-sided spectrally negative \(3/2\)-stable motion after completed-graph quantile inversion. The local process theorem, the \(n^{1/4}\) peak-location law, and the data-only disjoint-block \(90\%\) interval hold uniformly for every subcritical clip \(\sqrt n\,b_n\to0\), including \(b_n=n^{-2/3}\). At the critical scale \(\sqrt n\,b_n\to\lambda\in(0,\infty)\), the capped jump law is explicit; the main class does not determine its clipping drift, while a stated boundary-trace subclass yields the full drifted process and peak law. At every vanishing supercritical clip \(\sqrt n\,b_n\to\infty\), two fixed legal witnesses have opposite nonzero \(b_n^{1/2}\)-order peak shifts, so the \(n^{1/4}\) roots are not uniformly tight. Thus \(n^{-1/2}\) is the sharp clipping boundary for the original stable peak law and its block calibration.
gap: The closest weak-overlap QTE result describes finitely many fixed percentiles, while regular QTE process theory is Gaussian. Neither result controls the shrinking percentile increments, inverse-graph centering, or global localization needed to infer where the QTE is largest.
fill: The project derives the marked local tail coefficient, proves a uniform completed-graph functional limit, localizes the empirical maximizer, identifies its stable-parabolic scaling law, and verifies the uniform root approximation needed for a disjoint-block interval.
